newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch join hunt for Nazi gold in Swiss banks.
newsitem.headline: Dutch join hunt for Nazi gold in Swiss banks.

text.p: The Netherlands said on Friday it may press a 50-year-old claim to a fortune in gold looted by the Nazis during World War Two if it is found to be still held in Swiss bank vaults.
But a finance ministry spokesman said there were formidable legal complexities surrounding the claim and the issue could take years to resolve.
"We have waited now for half a century so a few more years is not really that long," he said.
After the war the Dutch claimed 145 tonnes of gold taken from the central bank and Dutch citizens by the occupying German army and allegedly transferred to Switzerland.

But, under a 1946 agreement between Switzerland and an Allied commission, the Dutch were compensated for only 70 tonnes and have never dropped their claim on the other 75 tonnes -- currently estimated to be worth around one billion dollars.

The claim has been reinvigorated by the Swiss government's decision to set up an experts committee empowered to lift the legendary veil of secrecy around the country's banks to produce an historical account of Swiss commerce with the Nazis.
Legislation already adopted by the Lower House of parliament in Berne and expected to clear the Upper House in December gives the committee five years to complete its work.

The enquiry is a response to mounting international pressure over allegations that Swiss banks, including the central bank, were repositories for Nazi plunder, including gold stolen from Holocaust victims and conquered countries.
A $20 billion class action suit was filed earlier this month in New York on behalf of Holocaust survivors against Swiss banks for allegedly refusing to return victims' assets.

And a British Foreign Office report released last month said the $60 million paid in 1946 to settle claims connected with Nazi gold was little more than a tenth of the gold thought to be in Swiss bank vaults at the end of the war.
The report said the director of the Swiss National Bank had let slip during the post-war negotiations that Swiss banks held $500 million when the war ended, worth $6.5 billion today.

The Dutch have started their own investigation into the issue, which will focus primarily on the tangled legal status of their claim, but any action is likely to depend on the findings of the Swiss committee, the finance ministry spokesman said.
"It depends on the Swiss. Maybe their conclusion will be that there is no gold and we can claim whatever we want but we won't get anything from them."
Switzerland has said all its legal obligations with regard to Nazi gold were settled by the 1946 agreement with the Allies.
